definition: Possible to do or carry out in practice with the time and resources available.
example: Working from home made it feasible for him to care for his grandmother.
nuance: Feasible stresses that something can really be done with the means at hand, while possible can mean merely conceivable.
prompt: A town council is deciding whether to build a footbridge over a creek.
options: With a state grant and volunteer labor, the footbridge finally looked feasible.
Engineers called the footbridge feasible after concluding it could never be built.
The old footbridge was so feasible that it wobbled under a single walker.
The council hired a feasible engineer who always arrived early to meetings.
reasons: Money and workers made the project practical to carry out.
A project that can never be built is the reverse of doable.
This confuses the word with feeble; it does not mean weak or flimsy.
The word describes plans or tasks, not a person's punctuality or character.

practice.prompt: A student is planning how to finish a science project before Friday.
options: Splitting the work into three short evenings made the deadline feasible.
Since the project needed a month of daily measurements, finishing by Friday was feasible.
Her poster board was too feasible to stand up and kept flopping over.
She felt feasible about her topic and couldn't wait to present it.
reasons: Breaking the task into manageable parts made it achievable in practice.
A month of work cannot fit into a few days, so the plan was not achievable.
Flimsiness is not the meaning; this mixes the word up with feeble.
The word does not describe feelings like eagerness or confidence.
